definitions.definition: A class of sacred narrative lore, called with itihāsa the 'fifth Veda'; remembered by Brahmā before the Vedas and condensed by Vyāsa in every Dvāpara age into eighteen Purāṇas of four lakh verses.
Traditional narrative (above all the Mahābhārata and Rāmāyaṇa), named with purāṇa as the fifth Veda.
One of the eighteen principal Purāṇas; the lists differ in naming the Śiva or the Vāyu and in their order (VP 3.6.21-23; BhP 12.7.23-24; KūP 1.1.13-15).
A Purāṇa outside the eighteen, said to have been told by sages or Vyāsa's disciples; the Kūrma lists eighteen; any Purāṇa taught apart from the eighteen has issued from them (Matsya 53.64).
The five marks of a Purāṇa: sarga, pratisarga, vaṃśa, manvantara and vaṃśānucarita.
The Bhāgavata's ten marks of a (great) Purāṇa, given in two different lists (BhP 2.10.1; 12.7.9-10); the tenth, āśraya/apāśraya, is the support for whose sake the other nine are told.
Primary creation: the arising of the principles (mahat, the elements, the senses) from the unmanifest (BhP 2.10.3; VP 1.5).
The second of the five marks; in most Purāṇic usage the secondary creation by Brahmā (and by some understood as dissolution and re-creation).
In the Bhāgavata, the secondary creation by Brahmā (the Puruṣa's creation) from the imbalance of the guṇas (BhP 2.10.3).
The genealogies of gods, sages and kings - the third mark of a Purāṇa.
The narratives of the kings of the solar and lunar dynasties - the fifth mark of a Purāṇa.
The bardic reciter of Purāṇa; Romaharṣaṇa and his son Ugraśravas are 'the Sūta' of the Purāṇic frames at Naimiṣa.
A reciter/teacher of the Purāṇas; the six paurāṇikas who learned from Romaharṣaṇa (BhP 12.7.5).
The root Purāṇa-saṃhitās: Romaharṣaṇa's and those of his three saṃhitā-making disciples (four in all).
A text or section glorifying a deity, place, time, vow or scripture and its fruits (e.g. Devī Māhātmya, Kāśī-māhātmya, Bhāgavata-māhātmya).
Local temple or place legend in Purāṇic form, often claiming to belong to a Mahāpurāṇa such as the Skanda.
The four verses spoken by the Lord to Brahmā (BhP 2.9.32-35), held to be the seed of the whole Bhāgavata.
The ritual hearing of the Bhāgavata in seven days, modelled on Śuka's recital to Parīkṣit and prescribed in the Bhāgavata-māhātmya.

An age of the world: Kṛta (Satya), Tretā, Dvāpara and Kali, of 4,000, 3,000, 2,000 and 1,000 divine years with junctions (sandhyā) of a tenth of that length before and after, so 4,800 + 3,600 + 2,400 + 1,200 divine years; dharma declines through them.
The first and best age (also Satya-yuga), when dharma stands on four feet and meditation (dhyāna) on Viṣṇu is the means.
The second age, in which sacrifice (yajña) is the principal means.
The third age, in which worship/service (paricaryā, arcana) is the principal means; in each Dvāpara a Vyāsa divides the Veda and condenses the Purāṇa.

The fourth and present age, an ocean of faults with one great virtue: that singing the Lord's name gives what meditation, sacrifice and worship gave in the earlier ages; reckoned by tradition from 3102 BCE.
A cycle of the four yugas (catur-yuga) of 12,000 divine years (4,320,000 human years).
A year of the gods, equal to 360 human years (a human year is a day and night of the gods).
A unit of 30 kalās; thirty muhūrtas make a human day and night (VP 1.3.8).
The period ruled by one Manu, about 71 cycles of the four yugas; fourteen make a day of Brahmā; each has its own Manu, Indra, gods, seven sages and avatāra.
Progenitor and law-giver presiding over a manvantara; the present is the seventh, Vaivasvata; the eighth will be Sāvarṇi (the Devī Māhātmya's Suratha).
A day of Brahmā of a thousand cycles of four yugas with fourteen Manus; his night of equal length is the occasional dissolution; each kalpa bears a name (e.g. the present Śveta-Vārāha).
Half of Brahmā's lifetime of a hundred years of such days and nights; the whole life (two parārdhas) ends in the elemental dissolution.
The dissolution of beings or worlds, fourfold: constant, occasional, elemental and final.
The continual arising and perishing of all beings, carried off by the current of time.
The dissolution of the three worlds at the end of Brahmā's day, while the creator sleeps on Ananta.
The dissolution at the end of Brahmā's life when the cosmic egg and all principles return into Prakṛti.
Liberation understood as a dissolution: knowledge cuts the ego-knot and the self abides in itself; dissolution into the eternal Brahman (VP 6.8.1).
The cosmic egg within which the fourteen worlds lie, enclosed by sheaths of the elements; broken up in the elemental dissolution.
In the Purāṇas the cosmic creator Brahmā as the first embodied being; in VP 6.7.51 the being whose contemplation is of both Brahman and action.
A world or plane of beings; the Purāṇas count fourteen within the egg - seven above from Bhūr to Satya and seven below.
Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ and Svar - the region dissolved in each occasional dissolution and within which the hells lie.
The fourth upper world, where the wise dwell for a kalpa; passed by the yogin's gradual ascent.
The highest world within the egg, Brahmā's world, lasting two parārdhas; the yogin who reaches it passes with Brahmā to liberation.
The seven netherworlds below the earth (bila-svarga), full of palaces, named differently in the Bhāgavata and the Viṣṇu Purāṇa; also the name of the lowest of them.
One of the seven concentric island-continents of Bhū-maṇḍala (Jambu, Plakṣa, Śālmali, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śāka, Puṣkara), each ringed by an ocean.
The central island-continent with Meru at its centre, divided into nine varṣas, Bhārata being the southern one.
The golden axial mountain at the centre of Jambudvīpa, with the cities of the gods on its summit; the VP gives it 84,000 yojanas above ground and 16,000 below.
The mountain range beyond the seventh ocean dividing the lit world from the dark regions beyond.
The region south of the Himālaya and north of the ocean, the one land of action (karma-bhūmi), where the gods wish to be born.
Bhārata, where deeds are done and bear fruit and liberation can be won; the other regions are lands of enjoyment.
The regions other than Bhārata, where beings only enjoy the fruits of past deeds.

A place of torment for the dead, below the earth in the south within the three worlds, ruled by Yama; twenty-eight are named in BhP 5.26; the VP also calls heaven what pleases the mind and hell its opposite.
The terrible river on the road to Yama, a hundred yojanas wide and full of pus and blood, crossed easily by those who gave the Vaitaraṇī cow; also one of the hells of BhP 5.26.
Yama (Dharmarāja, Vaivasvata), king of the ancestors, who judges the dead according to their deeds under the Lord's command; he has no authority over the Lord's devotees.
The fearsome servants of Yama who bind and drag the dead to Yama's city; they appear to the dying.
Servants of Viṣṇu who protect a dying person who has uttered the Lord's name from Yama's messengers.
Yama's recorder of the deeds of beings, consulted at judgment.
The departure of the living being from the body at death; for the yogin a controlled departure through the crown.
The subtle being, the size of a thumb, drawn out of the body at death by Yama's messengers.
The airy (vāyavīya) body that the dead takes immediately upon leaving the gross body.
The body of the preta built up limb by limb by the ten days' piṇḍas, which merges with the airy body.
The body, born of one's deeds and not of parents, in which the dead is bound and suffers on the road and in hell.
The newly dead before being joined with the ancestors; one whose rites are lacking (e.g. no vṛṣotsarga) or who did great wrong remains a preta, hungry and thirsty, troubling kin.

literal: one who has gone forth; the departed

definitions.definition: The ancestors, to whose company the dead is joined by sapiṇḍīkaraṇa and who are fed by śrāddha; they dwell in the south below the earth.
The rice-ball offered to the dead and ancestors; the ten daily piṇḍas build the preta's body and the monthly ones feed him on the road.
The rite of offering food and water to the dead and the ancestors (ekoddiṣṭa for one preta, pārvaṇa for the three ancestors), with feeding of brahmins.
The sets of sixteen śrāddhas for the newly dead before and after sapiṇḍīkaraṇa (the 'soiled', 'middle' and 'highest' sixteen).
The rite that joins the preta to the three generations of ancestors, ending the preta state; done on the twelfth day or up to a year after death.
The rite of setting free a consecrated bull on the eleventh day, without which the preta state becomes fixed.
The rite performed for one who died a bad or untimely death so that the normal rites can take effect.
A sign foretelling death, by which yogins know their time (e.g. no longer seeing Arundhatī or the pole-star).

The one possessing the six excellences - lordship, valour, fame, fortune, knowledge and detachment - who knows the origin and end of beings, knowledge and ignorance; properly Vāsudeva; with Brahman and Paramātman one of three names of the non-dual reality.
The six excellences whose possessor is Bhagavat: aiśvarya, vīrya, yaśas, śrī, jñāna, vairāgya.
In the Bhāgavata one of the three names of the non-dual reality (with Brahman and Bhagavān).

A descent of the Lord in a form for the protection of the world; innumerable, the principal ones listed as twenty-two (BhP 1.3), ten (Agni, Garuḍa) and in other lists; all are portions and parts, but Kṛṣṇa is Bhagavān himself (BhP 1.3.28).

The Lord's free, purposeless-yet-gracious activity in creation and in the avatāras, above all Kṛṣṇa's play in Vraja; VP 6.7.71-72 says his activity is not caused by karma but is for the good of the worlds.
Kṛṣṇa's circle dance with the gopīs on the autumn full-moon night (BhP 10.29-33).

literal: the play of the rāsa dance

definitions.definition: The women of Vraja whose love for Kṛṣṇa, in union and separation, is the Bhāgavata's model of devotion.
Love in separation from the beloved Lord, which keeps the mind constantly on him (BhP 10.47.34).
Absorption in or identity with the object of constant attention; reached by any strong emotion directed at Hari.

Unmotivated, uninterrupted love and service directed to the Lord, the highest dharma (BhP 1.2.6); graded by the guṇas and beyond them (3.29); ninefold in practice (7.5.23-24); the one means that 'wins' the Lord (11.14.20-21).
Devotion without any motive of gain, which does not even seek liberation.
The unbroken flow of the mind to the Lord on merely hearing of his qualities, like the Gaṅgā into the sea (BhP 3.29.11-12).
The nine forms: hearing, singing, remembering, serving the feet, worship, obeisance, servitude, friendship and self-offering (BhP 7.5.23-24).
Hearing the Lord's names, qualities and deeds, the first form of devotion and the beginning of the path (BhP 1.2.16-21); for the Śiva Purāṇa the first of the three great means.
Singing or reciting the Lord's names and deeds, the chief means of the Kali age.
Remembering the Lord, the third form of devotion, and the supreme expiation (VP 2.6.39-40).
Service of the Lord's feet, the fourth form of devotion.
Ritual worship of the Lord, the fifth form of devotion; the chief means in the Dvāpara age.
Bowing to and praising the Lord, the sixth form of devotion.
The attitude and practice of being the Lord's servant, the seventh form of devotion.
Friendship with the Lord, the eighth form of devotion.
Complete self-surrender to the Lord, the ninth form of devotion.
In the Śiva Purāṇa the third and greatest of the three means (hearing, singing, reflecting on Śiva).
A devotee of the Lord; the Bhāgavata Purāṇa; devotees are themselves tīrthas (BhP 1.13.10).
The practices of devotion to Bhagavān, to be undertaken from childhood (BhP 7.6.1).
The twelve who know the Lord's dharma: Brahmā, Nārada, Śambhu, Kumāra, Kapila, Manu, Prahlāda, Janaka, Bhīṣma, Bali, Śuka and Yama.
The Lord's name, whose utterance, even indirect, destroys sins and is the supreme expiation and the dharma of the age.
One of ten offences that obstruct the fruit of chanting the name, listed from the Padma Purāṇa by later Vaiṣṇava authors.
The rite that removes sin; the Purāṇas hold the name or remembrance of the Lord to be the best expiation.
Taking refuge in the Lord or the Goddess, as Gajendra and the gods do; the Goddess is 'intent on saving those who come for refuge'.
Liberation as residence in the Lord's world; one of five liberations devotees do not accept without service.
Liberation as equal lordship/opulence with the Lord.
Liberation as proximity to the Lord.
Liberation as having a form like the Lord's.
Liberation as union/oneness (ekatva) with the Lord; reached even by Śiśupāla through enmity (VP 4.15.2).
Liberation by stages: the yogin ascends to Satyaloka and is liberated with Brahmā at the dissolution (BhP 2.2.22-31).
Liberation at once at death, as opposed to the gradual ascent.
Śiva's sign: the manifest (unmanifest Prakṛti) whose root is the unmarked Śiva; the formless (niṣkala) liṅga of worship; the column of fire.
Śiva as partless Brahman, worshipped in the formless liṅga.
Śiva as having form, worshipped in the image.
The twelve self-manifest liṅgas of Śiva's radiance in sacred sites, told in the Śiva Purāṇa's Koṭirudra Saṃhitā.
Śiva's mantra 'namaḥ śivāya' (six syllables with Oṃ), praised as the essence of the Veda.
The night of Śiva's worship (esp. the great one in Māgha/Phālguna), kept with fast and vigil.
Sacred ash worn by Śaivas (often as the tripuṇḍra), praised in the Śiva Purāṇa.
The seed worn and used for japa by Śaivas, glorified in the Śiva Purāṇa (Vidyeśvara 25) and the Devī Bhāgavata.
In the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā the highest of five yogas: contemplation of Śiva's own nature alone, without adjuncts.
The Goddess as the power that deludes even the wise and creates the world, and when pleased grants liberation.
The Lord's sleep on the waters between creations; in the Devī Māhātmya the Goddess as Viṣṇu's sleep who leaves him so he can wake.
Kālī's name after slaying Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa (DM 7).
The powers of Brahmā, Śiva, Skanda, Viṣṇu, Varāha, Narasiṃha and Indra appearing as goddesses who fight beside the Goddess and are absorbed into her.
The nine-night worship of the Goddess, especially in autumn (the 'great worship' of DM 12).
The Goddess's supreme abode beyond the worlds, described in the Devī Bhāgavata.
The Goddess Tripurasundarī of the Lalitopākhyāna, who arises from the gods' sacrificial fire to slay Bhaṇḍāsura.
Lalitā's city (Śrīnagara) with its enclosures and the Cintāmaṇi palace at the centre.

VP 6.7.31: the joining with Brahman of the special, effort-dependent movement of the mind; LiP 1.8: restraint of citta's activities, and the word means nirvāṇa, Maheśa's state; ŚiP 7.2.37.6: the mind's steady activity fixed on Śiva.
The first limb: in the VP and ŚiP non-harming, truth, non-stealing, celibacy, non-possession; in MkP 41.16 the ascetic's five vows (non-stealing, celibacy, renunciation, non-greed, non-harming).
The second limb: VP study, purity, contentment, austerity; ŚiP purity, contentment, austerity, japa, praṇidhi; MkP freedom from anger, service to the teacher, purity, light food, study.
Posture; the Vāyavīya names eight (svastika, padma, ardhendu, vīra, yoga, prasādhita, paryaṅka, as one likes); the MkP names padma, half and svastika.
Mastery of the breath, in recaka, pūraka, kumbhaka; with or without support; it burns the faults (BhP 3.28.11) and yields the states of calm and clarity (ŚiP 7.2.39).
VP 6.7.40-42: prāṇāyāma is with a support (the gross form of the Lord as its object) or without.
Drawing the senses back from objects so they follow the mind, as a tortoise draws in its limbs.
Fixing the mind on a support - the Lord's form (VP, BhP) or bodily places and the subtle elements (MkP).
VP 6.7.91: one continuous flow of the form's awareness, desiring nothing else; ŚiP 7.2.39: with object and then without.
VP 6.7.92: the grasping of the very nature of the object free of imagination, produced by meditation.
The support of the mind in yoga: Viṣṇu's form, the ground of all powers, which alone purifies (VP 6.7.45-78).
VP 6.7.48-51: the three contemplations of beings - of Brahman, of action, and of both.
ŚiP 7.2.39.8-10: meditation resting on a form (with seed) and awareness of the formless self (without seed).

Obstacle-powers that arise after the gross obstacles are overcome: in MkP longings for rewards and five states (prātibha, śrāvaṇa, daiva, bhrama, āvarta); in LiP/ŚiP six siddhis (pratibhā, śravaṇa, vārtā, darśana, āsvāda, vedanā).
An obstacle on the path of yoga; the ten of LiP 1.9 and ŚiP 7.2.38; the powers themselves are antarāyas (BhP 11.15.33).
Powers arising from dhāraṇā - eighteen in the Bhāgavata, eight aiśvaryas in MkP and LiP - which are obstacles to the highest goal.
The syllable Oṃ, whose three measures and half-measure are meditated upon; raised in the heart like a bell's sound.
The fourth, half measure of Oṃ, beyond the guṇas and beyond speech, touched at the crown (MkP 42.5-6, 42.14).
The opening at the crown through which the yogin departs.
In BhP 2.2.24 the brilliant path by which the departing yogin rises to Vaiśvānara.

In the Purāṇas the calm of the mind freed of object like a flame going out (BhP 3.28.35), the end of the delusion of object-knowledge-action (11.14.46), Maheśa's state (LiP 1.8.5), and the self's nature (VP 6.7.22).
Freedom from attachment; the supreme dispassion by which the upasarga-powers are renounced (LiP 1.9.52-56).
In the Purāṇas the supreme reality, identified with Viṣṇu (VP), Śiva (ŚiP), or the Goddess (DBhP); one of three names of non-dual knowledge (BhP 1.2.11).
The Lord's power by which what is not real appears (BhP 2.9.33); the gross and subtle forms are fashioned by its guṇas (1.3.30).
Power: the world as the power of Brahman like light from a fire (VP 1.22.56); Viṣṇu's threefold śakti (VP 6.7.61); the Goddess herself (DM).
VP 6.7.11: taking non-self for self and what is not one's own as 'mine'; VP 1.5.5: fivefold avidyā arising first in creation; VP 6.7.61: the third, 'avidyā-karma' śakti.
The sense of 'mine', root of suffering (MkP 38.6), one of the two forms of ignorance (VP 6.7.11).
In the VP the lower (aparā) śakti of Viṣṇu, the embodied knower veiled by avidyā-karma; in MkP 38.15 the self other than the aggregate of guṇas.
The mind, cause of bondage when attached to objects and of liberation when free of them (VP 6.7.28).
Primal matter, one of the four forms of Viṣṇu in the VP (with puruṣa, vyakta and kāla).
Nature whose properties (suffering, ignorance) belong to it and not to the self (VP 6.7.22-24); the Goddess as the primordial unmanifest Prakṛti (DM 4).
The cosmic Person with sixteen parts, source of the avatāras (BhP 1.3.1); spirit as one of the four forms of Viṣṇu (VP 1.2).
Time, a form of Viṣṇu that joins and separates pradhāna and puruṣa (VP 1.2); the Lord's form that carries off all beings (BhP 12.4.36-38).
The three qualities of Prakṛti (sattva, rajas, tamas) by which devotion (BhP 3.29), Purāṇas (Matsya 53.68-69) and the measures of Oṃ (MkP 42.4) are classified.
The afflictions, whose destruction comes by yoga alone (VP 6.7.25).
Suffering from oneself (body and mind), from other beings, and from divine/natural powers (VP 6.5.1-6).
Karma that has begun to fruit and keeps the body of the liberated alive until exhausted (BhP 3.28.38: 'the body ... lives on while its karma lasts').
The Bhāgavata names kaivalya as its sole purpose (BhP 12.13.12).
Austerity, for which (not for sense-pleasure) the human body is meant (BhP 5.5.1).
The one Lord as Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva for creation, maintenance and destruction (VP 1.2.66); in Śākta Purāṇas the three receive their power from the Goddess.
A holy place of pilgrimage and bathing; the virtues are inner tīrthas and the purest mind the supreme tīrtha; devotees are living tīrthas.
Truth, forbearance, sense-control, compassion and the other virtues as tīrthas; purity of mind the highest.
A holy person who, carrying the Lord within, makes even the tīrthas holy.
A sacred territory such as Kāśī or Puruṣottama; seven cities are liberating (GP 2.38.5).
A religious vow for a set period or day (fast, vigil, worship, gifts), with its story and fruit (e.g. Ekādaśī, Śivarātri, Navarātra, Kātyāyanī vrata).
Fasting as part of a vow.
The eleventh lunar day of each fortnight, kept with fasting for Viṣṇu; so powerful by the Nārada's praise that Yama's realm was emptied.
Religious giving, especially to brahmins; at death the gifts (cow, land, sesame etc.) ease the road of the dead.
The sixteen great gifts described in the Matsya and other Purāṇas.
The first great gift: gold (or other goods) equal to the donor's weight.
